power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "For example, Chinese Desirability ratings for infant item Iv3 (peeking into a bag) exceeded Japanese ratings by 1.11 points, p = .007, whereas Japanese ratings for S1 (showing interest in properties of objects) exceeded both Chinese ratings by 0.59 points and German ratings by 0.97 points (both p < .05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: Recognizing versus valuing curiosity: Cross-country similarities and differences in parental judgments of early curious behaviors Author Names and Affiliations

text.text: Cross-cultural research has examined whether parents differ in how they value curiosity as a developmental characteristic, but it remains unclear whether they understand the concept in the same way.
Because early curiosity must be inferred from behavior, concrete behavioral judgments offer a direct test of this question.

Parents in Germany, China, and Japan were randomly assigned to judge age-appropriate behaviors from a published infant-toddler or earlychildhood curiosity measure, rating each either as an expression of curiosity or as socially desirable.
The 689 parents (142 German, 425 Chinese, and 122 Japanese; ethnicity not explicitly collected) reported on children aged 5 to 71 months (344 girls, 345 boys) between July 2025 and March 2026.

Candidate curiosity items clearly outperformed non-curiosity fillers in every country (differences of 1.19 to 2.84 points on a 7-point scale), and behavior orderings were strongly similar across countries (Spearman ρ = .67 to .88).

Ratings were near-identical for individual items such as poking and probing, with country differences in curiosity attribution occurring much less compared to desirability differences (for 4 versus 19 items).
These findings suggest that cultures may differ less in what curiosity looks like than in which behavioral expressions of curiosity are welcomed and reinforced.
Curiosity helps young children learn, but adults cannot see curiosity directly-they must infer it from what children do, such as exploring objects, asking questions, or trying new actions.
Previous research has asked whether parents in different cultures value curiosity, but less is known about whether they understand the same behaviors as expressions of it.
We asked parents in Germany, China, and Japan to judge early-childhood behaviors either for how much they expressed curiosity or how socially desirable they were.
Parents largely agreed on which behaviors were curious, but differed more in how positively they viewed them.
This suggests that cultural differences may lie less in what curiosity looks like and more in which curious behaviors are welcomed and reinforced.
Curiosity is often treated as an important driver of children's learning, but it is not obvious what curiosity looks like in early childhood.

Even within psychological research, curiosity has been described in different ways, including interest in novelty, information seeking, uncertainty reduction, exploratory behavior, question asking, and engagement with the environment (Jirout et al., 2024; Loewenstein, 1994).
text.formatted: Even within psychological research, curiosity has been described in different ways, including interest in novelty, information seeking, uncertainty reduction, exploratory behavior, question asking, and engagement with the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Jirout et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Loewenstein, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: These theoretical distinctions are useful, but they also highlight a more basic question for developmental research.

When a young child looks closely at an unfamiliar object, takes objects out of a container, follows another person's actions, asks repeated questions, or tries out a new activity, do adults see the same underlying construct?
In early childhood, curiosity cannot usually be assessed through children's explicit self-reports.
It has to be inferred from behavior, and parents are among the people who make these inferences most often.
Parents' interpretations matter because they are likely to shape how curiosity is supported in everyday life.
A behavior that is recognized as curiosity may be noticed, scaffolded, and encouraged, whereas the same behavior may be redirected if it is seen as disruptive, risky, or socially inappropriate.
At the same time, recognising a behavior as curious is not the same as wanting to see more of it.

A child who takes apart an object, investigates someone else's belongings, or asks many questions may be trying to learn something, but parents may differ in whether they view such behavior as desirable and worth encouraging.

Thus, parents' judgments of early curiosity involve at least two related but separable questions: whether a behavior is understood as an expression of curiosity, and whether that behavior is evaluated positively.
Most cross-cultural research on curiosity has not directly separated these questions.

Existing studies have examined whether parents regard curiosity as an important child characteristic, often alongside broader developmental qualities such as independence, selfconfidence, creativity, or approaches to learning (Chuang & Su, 2009; Jose et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Existing studies have examined whether parents regard curiosity as an important child characteristic, often alongside broader developmental qualities such as independence, selfconfidence, creativity, or approaches to learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chuang & Su, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Jose et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Other work has investigated parenting goals and practices that may support exploration, autonomy, learning, or social engagement (Bornstein et al., 1992; Keller et al., 2006; Lansford et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Other work has investigated parenting goals and practices that may support exploration, autonomy, learning, or social engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bornstein et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Keller et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Lansford et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These studies show that curiosity-related values and socialization goals can be studied across cultural contexts, but they do not tell us whether parents identify the same concrete behaviors as curiosity in the first place.

A related line of work has developed and validated caregiver-report questionnaires of early curiosity across different language and cultural contexts (Altmann, et al., 2025; Altmann, de Boer, et al., 2026; Eiteljoerge & Altmann, 2026; Lee et al., 2023; Passaquindici et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A related line of work has developed and validated caregiver-report questionnaires of early curiosity across different language and cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Altmann, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Altmann, de Boer, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Eiteljoerge & Altmann, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lee et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Passaquindici et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Tang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These studies are important because they show that individual differences in curiosity can be measured meaningfully in more than one context.
At the same time, questionnaire validation starts from an already specified operationalization of the construct.

It can show whether a set of items functions psychometrically, but it does not by itself answer whether parents across contexts intuitively understand those behaviors as curiosity, nor whether they would want to encourage them in daily life.
Distinguishing these judgments is developmentally important.

If parents across contexts recognize similar behaviors as curiosity, this would suggest some shared understanding of how early curiosity is expressed, even before children can explain their own motives.

If parents differ mainly in whether they welcome those behaviors, cultural variation in curiosity may emerge less from recognising different forms of curiosity and more from how particular expressions are encouraged, tolerated, or redirected over time.
Conversely, if parents differ in which behaviors they recognize as curiosity at all, then cross-cultural differences may begin already at the level of interpreting children's actions.
In either case, parental judgments provide a plausible link between cultural beliefs and the everyday behavioral forms through which children's curiosity develops.

Germany, China, and Japan provide an informative comparison because they differ in socialization goals and parenting practices that may be relevant to children's exploratory behavior, while also allowing us to move beyond a simple East-West contrast.

German middleclass parenting is often described as relatively autonomy-oriented, with an emphasis on children's independent exploration, verbal engagement, and self-expression (Keller et al., 2006; Keller & Demuth, 2006).
text.formatted: German middleclass parenting is often described as relatively autonomy-oriented, with an emphasis on children's independent exploration, verbal engagement, and self-expression <ref type="bibr">(Keller et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Keller & Demuth, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In such a context, behaviors that signal self-initiated exploration or active information seeking may be especially likely to be encouraged, although this does not imply that all forms of exploration are equally welcomed.
Chinese parenting has often been discussed in relation to Confucian traditions of learning, effort, family obligation, and respect for adult guidance.

Yet, contemporary urban Chinese parenting cannot be reduced to authoritarian control or collectivism, and recent work shows both warmth and high involvement alongside stronger academic and training goals than are typically emphasized in Western European samples (Chao, 2001; Dong et al., 2023; He et al., 2021; Keller et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Yet, contemporary urban Chinese parenting cannot be reduced to authoritarian control or collectivism, and recent work shows both warmth and high involvement alongside stronger academic and training goals than are typically emphasized in Western European samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chao, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Dong et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">He et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Keller et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: These patterns make it plausible that parents may value curiosity when it is linked to learning and focused knowledge acquisition, while evaluating some behaviors differently when they appear to challenge adult authority, disrupt routines, or conflict with social expectations.
Japanese parenting is also often described as interdependence-oriented, but it differs from Chinese parenting in ways that are relevant for the present study.

Japanese socialization has been linked to empathy, group harmony, observational learning, and children's gradual internalization of self-control, with caregivers often supporting children through indirect guidance and close attunement rather than overt instruction alone (Bornstein et al., 1992; Holloway & Nagase, 2014; Rothbaum et al., 2000a Rothbaum et al., , 2000b)).
text.formatted: Japanese socialization has been linked to empathy, group harmony, observational learning, and children's gradual internalization of self-control, with caregivers often supporting children through indirect guidance and close attunement rather than overt instruction alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bornstein et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Holloway & Nagase, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Rothbaum et al., 2000a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Rothbaum et al., , 2000b))</ref>.

text.text: These features make it plausible that behaviors involving careful observation, social attunement, and context-sensitive exploration may be interpreted and evaluated differently from more disruptive or assertive forms of curiosity.
At the same time, none of these contexts should be treated as homogeneous, and broad cultural models cannot determine how individual parents will judge particular behaviors.

This caution is especially important because some of the cross-cultural parenting studies most relevant to the present comparison were conducted several decades ago, whereas contemporary families in all three countries are shaped by education, urbanization, changing gender roles, and globalized ideas about child development.
Within-country variation in parenting values and attitudes can also be substantial (Lansford et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Within-country variation in parenting values and attitudes can also be substantial <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Lansford et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The present study therefore does not use Germany, China, and Japan to represent fixed cultural types or to derive precise country-level predictions from earlier cultural models.

Instead, these samples provide a way to examine three more specific questions: (i) whether parents recognize the same concrete behaviors as expressions of curiosity, (ii) whether they differ in how positively they evaluate those behaviors, and (iii) whether any emerging differences are broad or concentrated in particular items.

To examine these questions, we asked parents to children from 5 months to 5 years of age to judge concrete, age-appropriate behaviors drawn from two validated caregiver-report measures of early curiosity: the Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire (ITCQ; Altmann, et al., 2025) and the Early Childhood Curiosity Questionnaire (ECCQ; Altmann, de Boer, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: To examine these questions, we asked parents to children from 5 months to 5 years of age to judge concrete, age-appropriate behaviors drawn from two validated caregiver-report measures of early curiosity: the Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire (ITCQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Altmann, et al., 2025)</ref> and the Early Childhood Curiosity Questionnaire (ECCQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Altmann, de Boer, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These questionnaires were well suited to the present purpose because they include diverse behaviors spanning sensory, investigative, and interactive expressions of early curiosity.
We included both, final questionnaire items and items that had been excluded during scale development, because both sets originated as candidate curiosity behaviors.
We also included filler items that were intentionally designed not to measure curiosity but instead covered behaviors more closely related to temperament, prosociality, routine, and neutral play.

Parents were randomly assigned to one of two judgment conditions: In the curiosity condition, parents indicated their agreement with the statement that the specific behavior was an expression of curiosity, whereas in the desirability condition, they indicated their agreement with the statement that it was socially desirable.
This design allowed us to compare two judgments that are often implicitly combined: whether a behavior is recognized as curiosity-related, and whether that behavior is evaluated positively.

The analyses addressed the research questions as follows: First, we examined whether candidate curiosity behaviors, including final and excluded questionnaire items, were rated more highly than intentionally non-curiosity filler behaviors.
Second, we tested whether parents in Germany, China, and Japan differed in their curiosity and desirability ratings.

Given cross-cultural differences in socialization goals and expectations about children's behavior, we expected differences to be especially likely for desirability, whereas agreement in curiosity recognition remained an open question.
Third, we examined whether cross-country differences were broad or concentrated in particular behaviors, especially if they received diverging ratings on either dimension across countries.

Country differences in Desirability were more frequent, occurring for 5 of 23 final ITCQ items and 14 of 25 final ECCQ items.
Overall, the larger differences often involved lower ratings in the German sample and higher ratings in the Chinese sample, although this was not a uniform country ordering across items.

For example, Chinese Desirability ratings for infant item Iv3 (peeking into a bag) exceeded Japanese ratings by 1.11 points, p = .007, whereas Japanese ratings for S1 (showing interest in properties of objects) exceeded both Chinese ratings by 0.59 points and German ratings by 0.97 points (both p < .05).

text.text: Among ECCQ items, some of the largest differences involved Iv4 (taking items out of containers) and N6 (pointing in new environments).
For both items, adjusted Desirability ratings were lowest in Germany (Iv4: Germany = 3.91, Japan = 5.09, China = 5.75; N6: Germany = 4.86, Japan = 6.27, China = 6.38).

The desirability-versus-curiosity contrast (computed as the adjusted Desirability mean minus the adjusted Curiosity mean within each country) describes how strongly a behavior was valued relative to how strongly it was recognized as curiosity within each country-level group.

text.text: Two final ITCQ items showed significant and practically meaningful country differences in this contrast.

For Iv1 (taking items out of containers) the German contrast was 1.43 points more negative than the Chinese contrast (95% CI [-2.33, -0.54], p = .041), indicating relatively lower Desirability compared with Curiosity ratings in the German sample.
On the other hand, for Iv3 (peeking into a bag), the Chinese contrast was 1.41 points more positive than the Japanese contrast (95% CI [0.67, 2.16], p = .016).

In the ECCQ, significant and practically meaningful country differences in the contrast occurred for nine final items across all subscales: N4, N6, N7, Iv4, Iv5, Iv6, Iv7, Ia5, and Ia8.

The largest involved Iv4 (taking items out of containers), for which the German contrast was more negative than both the Japanese (difference = -1.83, 95% CI [-2.92, -0.74], p = .017) and the Chinese contrast (difference = -1.57, 95% CI [-2.36, -0.79], p = .004).

German contrasts were also more negative than both other countries for N6 (pointing in new environments; Japan: difference = -1.54, p = .004; China: difference = -1.43, p < .001), and more negative than Japan for N7 (feeling new textures; difference = -1.49, p = .010), and Iv7 (doing little experiments; difference = -1.54, p = .028).

text.text: Child age was not associated with ratings in either questionnaire (ITCQ: b = -0.017, 95% CI [-0.068, 0.034], p = .507; ECCQ: b = -0.020, 95% CI [-0.067, 0.026], p = .393).
The estimated difference in ECCQ Curiosity ratings between boys and girls was small but did not survive false discovery rate correction (difference = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.04], p = .189).

One education contrast survived correction: in the ITCQ Desirability condition, the upper-secondaryor-below category made higher ratings than the undergraduate or bachelor reference category (difference = 0.58, 95% CI [0.12, 1.05], p = .044).
The remaining education contrasts were not significant after correction.

Across Germany, China, and Japan, parents showed considerable agreement about which concrete behaviors expressed early curiosity, while country differences were more common in judgments of desirability.
Meaningful Curiosity differences involved two final items in each questionnaire, compared with five infant and toddler (ITCQ) and fourteen preschool (ECCQ) items for Desirability.
Several behaviors also differed across countries in the extent to which their Desirability ratings stood above or below their Curiosity ratings.

The distinction between recognizing and valuing curiosity therefore mattered empirically: an action could be identified as curiosity-related without receiving equally positive evaluation across settings.
This pattern was not assumed at the outset.

Existing validation studies establish that caregiver-report curiosity measures can function across several national and language contexts, but they do not show that parents necessarily identify the same individual behaviors as manifestations of curiosity.

The present item profiles provide initial evidence that many of these concrete behaviors were interpreted similarly across the three samples, with strong rank-order correlations and very few practically meaningful Curiosity differences among final items.
At the same time, this agreement should not be interpreted as evidence that early curiosity is culturally universal in its behavioral expression.
The questionnaires necessarily sample a finite set of behaviors generated within an existing measurement program, and locally generated behaviors may reveal expressions that are not represented here.
Nevertheless, each age group included at least 50 diverse behaviors and situations, thereby offering a meaningful depth into the construct.

The more frequent Desirability differences are compatible with accounts in which socialization goals shape how caregivers respond to children's behavior (Keller et al., 2006), but the observed country pattern does not support a simple contrast between permissive Western and restrictive East Asian parenting.
text.formatted: The more frequent Desirability differences are compatible with accounts in which socialization goals shape how caregivers respond to children's behavior <ref type="bibr">(Keller et al., 2006</ref>), but the observed country pattern does not support a simple contrast between permissive Western and restrictive East Asian parenting.

text.text: German parents often provided the lower Desirability ratings, and item-level differences varied in direction.
In another behavioral domain, Runge and Soellner (2024) similarly linked socialization goals to differences in parents' evaluations of identical problem-behavior vignettes.
text.formatted: In another behavioral domain, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Runge and Soellner (2024)</ref> similarly linked socialization goals to differences in parents' evaluations of identical problem-behavior vignettes.

text.text: Such findings make the meaning of particular actions more informative than a general ranking of cultures by how much they support curiosity.

The present study did, however, not measure such socialization goals, safety concerns, privacy expectations, or situational norms that parents may have brought to individual items, so these explanations remain hypotheses for future work.
The difference between the two age-targeted questionnaires also raises a developmental possibility that deserves direct testing.
Desirability differences and country differences in the desirability-versus-curiosity contrasts were more frequent in the preschool questionnaire than in the infant and toddler questionnaire.

As children become capable of a wider range of self- directed, verbal, and socially consequential forms of exploration, there may be more opportunities for caregivers to encourage some expressions while redirecting others.
Repeated responses could, in principle, shape which forms of curiosity children increasingly express.
The present design, however, cannot demonstrate such an age-related trajectory because the questionnaires contain different items and were completed by different samples.
Longitudinal work that follows comparable behaviors across development is needed before stronger developmental conclusions can be drawn.
The distinction between recognition and desirability is also relevant to questionnaire interpretation.

Curiosity measures do not invariably reproduce identical structures across samples; for example, Kaneko (2022) did not recover distinct interest-and deprivation-type factors in Swedish preschoolers, whereas Tang et al. (2024) supported this distinction in young Chinese children.
These separate studies do not isolate culture as the explanation, but they illustrate why successful translation is not sufficient to establish equivalent measurement.
Likewise, similar item rankings in the present study do not demonstrate measurement invariance (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016).
text.formatted: Likewise, similar item rankings in the present study do not demonstrate measurement invariance <ref type="bibr">(Putnick & Bornstein, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: An item may be widely recognized as curiosity-related yet describe behavior that is differently encouraged, permitted, or reported across settings.

If future validations identify non-invariant loadings or response thresholds, item-level information about perceived curiosity and desirability may help generate hypotheses about the source of that misfit, alongside alternatives such as translation or response-style differences.
Several limitations constrain interpretation.
The self-selected samples were drawn from particular recruitment contexts in Göttingen, Hangzhou, and Osaka, and cannot represent the internal diversity of Germany, China, or Japan.

Furthermore, ethnicity was not measured in a harmonized way across sites, while education differed markedly between samples, with the German model sample in particular containing a high proportion of postgraduate respondents.
The country samples and randomized condition cells were also unequal in size.

The mixedeffects models accommodate unbalanced data and the item-level models used HC3 robust covariance estimates, so that no downsampling was required; nevertheless, smaller cells provide less precise estimates and reduce power to detect modest differences.
Cultural response styles may contribute to absolute rating differences (Lamm & Keller, 2007), and the neutral questionnaire introduction cannot eliminate evaluative response tendencies.
text.formatted: Cultural response styles may contribute to absolute rating differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lamm & Keller, 2007)</ref>, and the neutral questionnaire introduction cannot eliminate evaluative response tendencies.

text.text: Finally, different parents rated Curiosity and Desirability, so the contrast analyses describe group-level patterns rather than discrepancies within individual parents.
Even though this was deliberate to avoid cross-contamination of either evaluation dimension, future work should relate these to each other within participants.

Conclusion To our knowledge, few studies have directly separated parents' recognition of concrete curiosity-related behaviors from their evaluation of whether those same behaviors are desirable across cultural contexts.
The present findings suggest substantial shared recognition within the behavior sets examined here, alongside more selective variation in how those behaviors are valued.

Associations between parental responsiveness and children's epistemic curiosity (Iwasaki et al., 2023) make caregiver responses a plausible developmental pathway, but the current data do not establish such an effect.

Future work combining locally generated behavioral examples, contextualized vignettes, qualitative accounts, and longitudinal observation could test when parental evaluations translate into differential encouragement or inhibition of children's exploration.
In this way, distinguishing what adults recognize as curiosity from what they wish children to do may help clarify how curiosity is expressed across development and sociocultural settings.

The final analytic sample comprised 689 parents from Germany (n = 142), China (n = 425), and Japan (n = 122; see Table 1 for details by country, questionnaire, and condition).

text.text: Children were between 5 and 71 months old (M = 31.17, SD = 17.92); 344 were girls and 345 were boys.
The proportion of respondents with a Bachelor's degree, equivalent qualification, or higher was 79.6% in Germany, 84.9% in China, and 73.0% in Japan.
In China, respondents were 21 to 40 years old, in Japan they were 25 to 45 years old, whereas this information was not collected for the German sample.
Furthermore, 98.6% of German children were reported as monolingual while the Chinese and Japanese samples were reportedly homogeneously monolingual.
Families in Germany were recruited through the developmental participant database at the University of Göttingen between December 2025 and March 2026.
Families in China were recruited through Hangzhou Normal University between July and September 2025.
Families in Japan were recruited through collaborating universities in Osaka between August and September 2025.
Participants received a small thank-you for completing the survey: a printable storybook in Germany, online credits worth RMB 60 in China, and an Amazon gift card worth JPY 600 in Japan.
Ethical approval was obtained at all participating sites before data collection, and parents provided informed consent before supplying any information.
